::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Is a point a neighbourhood?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1110428/is-a-point-a-neighbourhood), asked by [Quantum spaghettification](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/203397/quantum-spaghettification) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-01-19; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> In this question https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/474746/can-a-neighbourhood-of-a-point-be-an-singleton-set The answers indicate that a point is a neigbourhood. But would this therefore not mean that every (continuous) function is analytic? Since the definition of an analytic function is one where the taylor series converges to $f(x)$ for $x$ in a neighbourhood of $x_0$ (the point we are considering). But a taylor series around $x_0$ will always converge on to $f(x_0)$ (if done as we are assuming around the point $x_0$) at $x=x_0$. Since $x_0$ is itself a neighbourhood then every function should be analytic.
:::

If points are open, the topology is called *discrete*: every subset is open. Therefore, every function on a discrete topological space is continuous.  

But that's about as far as you can go and still say something interesting.  If $Y$ is a normed linear space (you need that or some similar structure in order to take a derivative), then $f\colon X \to Y$ is differentiable in the sense that
$$\lim_{x\to a} \frac{\Vert f(x) - f(a)\Vert}{d(x,a)}$$
exists.  On the other hand, the numerator tends to zero, while the denominator is one whenever $x\neq a$.  Therefore this limit is 0 for any $f$.

So yes, every function is differentiable, but every derivative is zero, which makes it not a very useful object.
